title: Advanced Algorithms
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 400L Advanced Algorithms curriculum: asymptotic analysis, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, graph algorithms (shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, max flow), amortized analysis, NP-completeness, and approximation/randomized algorithms, consistent with a rigorous CS algorithms sequence following an introductory data structures/algorithms course.

questions.question: What does it mean for an algorithm to run in O(n log n) time?
options: Its running time grows no faster than a constant multiple of n log n as input size n increases
It always takes exactly n log n operations regardless of input
It runs in constant time for all inputs
It requires n log n bytes of memory only
questions.correct_answer: Its running time grows no faster than a constant multiple of n log n as input size n increases
questions.explanation: Big-O notation gives an asymptotic upper bound on growth rate, meaning the algorithm's time does not exceed c*n log n for large n and some constant c.

questions.question: What is the difference between Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta notation?
options: Big-O is an upper bound, Big-Omega is a lower bound, and Big-Theta is a tight bound (both upper and lower)
They are all identical notations with different symbols
Big-O is a lower bound and Big-Omega is an upper bound
Big-Theta only applies to recursive algorithms
questions.correct_answer: Big-O is an upper bound, Big-Omega is a lower bound, and Big-Theta is a tight bound (both upper and lower)
questions.explanation: Big-O bounds growth from above, Big-Omega bounds it from below, and Big-Theta applies when both bounds match, giving an exact asymptotic characterization.

questions.question: Using the Master Theorem, what is the time complexity of a recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
questions.correct_answer: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: This recurrence fits Case 2 of the Master Theorem (a=2, b=2, f(n)=n matches n^log_b(a)=n), giving T(n) = O(n log n), as in merge sort.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the divide-and-conquer algorithm for finding the closest pair of points in a plane?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
questions.correct_answer: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: The classic closest-pair algorithm recursively divides points, solves subproblems, and merges using a strip check bounded by a constant number of comparisons per point, achieving O(n log n).

questions.question: What is the key idea behind dynamic programming?
options: Breaking a problem into overlapping subproblems and storing their solutions to avoid redundant computation
Always choosing the locally optimal choice at each step without reconsideration
Solving a problem by trying every possible permutation exhaustively
Using recursion without any memoization or storage of results
questions.correct_answer: Breaking a problem into overlapping subproblems and storing their solutions to avoid redundant computation
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming exploits overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, caching (memoizing) subproblem results to avoid recomputation, unlike plain divide-and-conquer.

questions.question: What is 'optimal substructure' as a property required for dynamic programming?
options: An optimal solution to the problem can be constructed from optimal solutions to its subproblems
The problem must have exactly one subproblem
The problem cannot be divided into smaller parts
Every subproblem must have a unique unrelated solution
questions.correct_answer: An optimal solution to the problem can be constructed from optimal solutions to its subproblems
questions.explanation: Optimal substructure means the globally optimal solution incorporates optimal solutions of its subproblems, which is necessary for dynamic programming to apply correctly.

questions.question: In the 0/1 Knapsack problem solved via dynamic programming, what is the time complexity using the standard table-based approach?
options: O(nW), where n is the number of items and W is the knapsack capacity
O(n log n)
O(2^n) always, with no improvement possible
O(n)
questions.correct_answer: O(nW), where n is the number of items and W is the knapsack capacity
questions.explanation: The DP table has dimensions n x W, and each cell is filled in constant time, giving pseudo-polynomial time complexity O(nW).

questions.question: What distinguishes a greedy algorithm from a dynamic programming approach?
options: A greedy algorithm makes a single locally optimal choice at each step without reconsidering previous choices, while DP considers overlapping subproblems
Greedy algorithms always explore all possible solutions exhaustively
Dynamic programming never revisits any subproblem
There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches
questions.correct_answer: A greedy algorithm makes a single locally optimal choice at each step without reconsidering previous choices, while DP considers overlapping subproblems
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms commit to the best immediate choice hoping it leads to a global optimum, whereas DP systematically evaluates subproblem combinations, which is necessary when the greedy choice property doesn't hold.

questions.question: What property must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to guarantee an optimal solution?
options: The greedy-choice property and optimal substructure
Only a large input size
The problem must be NP-complete
The problem must have no subproblems
questions.correct_answer: The greedy-choice property and optimal substructure
questions.explanation: A greedy algorithm produces a globally optimal solution only if the problem exhibits the greedy-choice property (a locally optimal choice leads to a global optimum) and optimal substructure.

questions.question: In Huffman coding, why are characters with higher frequency assigned shorter codes?
options: To minimize the total weighted length (and thus overall size) of the encoded message
To make the algorithm run faster regardless of output size
Because shorter codes are always easier to encrypt
To ensure every character has a code of the same length
questions.correct_answer: To minimize the total weighted length (and thus overall size) of the encoded message
questions.explanation: Huffman coding greedily builds a prefix-free binary tree that assigns shorter bit strings to more frequent symbols, minimizing the expected encoded length.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm using a binary heap priority queue?
options: O((V + E) log V)
O(V + E)
O(V^2 log E)
questions.correct_answer: O((V + E) log V)
questions.explanation: With a binary heap, each of the V extract-min operations costs O(log V) and each of the E edge relaxations may trigger a decrease-key in O(log V), giving O((V+E) log V).

questions.question: Why can't Dijkstra's algorithm be used correctly on graphs with negative edge weights?
options: It assumes once a vertex's shortest distance is finalized it cannot be improved, which negative weights can violate
Dijkstra's algorithm cannot handle any weighted graph at all
Negative weights make the graph disconnected automatically
Dijkstra's algorithm only works on trees, not general graphs
questions.correct_answer: It assumes once a vertex's shortest distance is finalized it cannot be improved, which negative weights can violate
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedy approach finalizes the shortest known distance to a vertex once dequeued, an invariant that negative edges can break by later producing a shorter path.

questions.question: What algorithm is used to find shortest paths in a graph that may contain negative edge weights (but no negative cycles)?
options: Bellman-Ford algorithm
Dijkstra's algorithm
Prim's algorithm
Kruskal's algorithm
questions.correct_answer: Bellman-Ford algorithm
questions.explanation: The Bellman-Ford algorithm correctly computes shortest paths even with negative edge weights by relaxing all edges V-1 times, and can also detect negative cycles.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the Bellman-Ford algorithm?
options: O(VE)
O(E log V)
O(V + E)
questions.correct_answer: O(VE)
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes all E edges in each of V-1 iterations, giving a time complexity of O(VE).

questions.question: What does the Floyd-Warshall algorithm compute?
options: All-pairs shortest paths between every pair of vertices in a weighted graph
Only the single-source shortest path from one vertex
The minimum spanning tree of a graph
The maximum flow through a network
questions.correct_answer: All-pairs shortest paths between every pair of vertices in a weighted graph
questions.explanation: Floyd-Warshall is a dynamic programming algorithm that computes shortest paths between all pairs of vertices, running in O(V^3) time.

questions.question: What is a minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected, weighted, undirected graph?
options: A subset of edges that connects all vertices with the minimum possible total edge weight and no cycles
A tree that contains only the highest-weight edges
Any subgraph containing all vertices and all edges
A tree with exactly one vertex and no edges
questions.correct_answer: A subset of edges that connects all vertices with the minimum possible total edge weight and no cycles
questions.explanation: An MST spans all vertices using the fewest edges (V-1 for V vertices) that form a tree while minimizing the sum of edge weights.

questions.question: How does Kruskal's algorithm construct a minimum spanning tree?
options: It sorts all edges by weight and greedily adds each edge that does not form a cycle, using a union-find structure
It starts from a single vertex and always adds the nearest unvisited vertex
It removes edges one at a time from the full graph until an MST remains
It requires the graph to be directed
questions.correct_answer: It sorts all edges by weight and greedily adds each edge that does not form a cycle, using a union-find structure
questions.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm is edge-based: it processes edges in increasing weight order and uses a disjoint-set (union-find) structure to detect and avoid cycles.

questions.question: How does Prim's algorithm construct a minimum spanning tree, in contrast to Kruskal's?
options: It grows the MST one vertex at a time, always adding the cheapest edge that connects a new vertex to the existing tree
It sorts all edges globally before doing anything else
It only works on directed acyclic graphs
It requires computing all-pairs shortest paths first
questions.correct_answer: It grows the MST one vertex at a time, always adding the cheapest edge that connects a new vertex to the existing tree
questions.explanation: Prim's algorithm is vertex-based, expanding a single growing tree by repeatedly adding the minimum-weight edge that connects a tree vertex to a non-tree vertex.

questions.question: What data structure is essential for an efficient implementation of Kruskal's algorithm to detect cycles?
options: Disjoint-set (union-find) data structure
A max-heap
A doubly linked list
A hash table alone
questions.correct_answer: Disjoint-set (union-find) data structure
questions.explanation: Union-find allows Kruskal's algorithm to efficiently check whether adding an edge would create a cycle by testing if its endpoints are already in the same connected component.

questions.question: What does the Ford-Fulkerson method compute in a flow network?
options: The maximum flow from a source vertex to a sink vertex
The shortest path between two vertices
The minimum spanning tree of the network
The chromatic number of the graph
questions.correct_answer: The maximum flow from a source vertex to a sink vertex
questions.explanation: Ford-Fulkerson repeatedly finds augmenting paths from source to sink in a residual graph and increases flow along them until no augmenting path remains, yielding the maximum flow.

questions.question: According to the Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem, what is true about the maximum flow in a network?
options: It equals the capacity of the minimum cut separating the source from the sink
It always equals the number of vertices in the graph
It is always infinite for connected graphs
It equals the number of edges in the graph
questions.correct_answer: It equals the capacity of the minimum cut separating the source from the sink
questions.explanation: The Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem states that the maximum feasible flow from source to sink equals the minimum total capacity of edges that, if removed, would disconnect the source from the sink.

questions.question: What is 'amortized analysis' used for in algorithm analysis?
options: Determining the average performance of an operation over a sequence of operations, even if individual operations vary in cost
Measuring only the worst possible single operation cost
Calculating the exact memory address of variables
Estimating compiler optimization levels
questions.correct_answer: Determining the average performance of an operation over a sequence of operations, even if individual operations vary in cost
questions.explanation: Amortized analysis averages the cost of expensive but infrequent operations over a sequence, giving a tighter bound than worst-case-per-operation analysis, as used in dynamic array resizing.

questions.question: In the amortized analysis of a dynamic array that doubles in size when full, what is the amortized cost per insertion?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
questions.explanation: Although occasional resizes cost O(n), doubling ensures resizes become increasingly rare, so the total cost over n insertions is O(n), giving an amortized O(1) per insertion.

questions.question: What does it mean for a decision problem to be in the complexity class P?
options: It can be solved by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time
It can only be solved by exhaustive brute force
It requires exponential time to solve on any computer
It cannot be solved by any algorithm
questions.correct_answer: It can be solved by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time
questions.explanation: Class P consists of decision problems solvable by a deterministic Turing machine (or standard computer) in time polynomial in the input size.

questions.question: What does it mean for a decision problem to be in the complexity class NP?
options: A proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time, even if finding the solution may take longer
It can never be solved by any computer
It is always solvable in polynomial time
It requires infinite memory to solve
questions.correct_answer: A proposed solution can be verified in polynomial time, even if finding the solution may take longer
questions.explanation: NP problems are those where, given a candidate solution (certificate), correctness can be verified by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time.

questions.question: What does it mean for a problem to be 'NP-complete'?
options: It is in NP and every other problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time
It can be solved in constant time
It is impossible to verify solutions for it
It belongs to class P by definition
questions.correct_answer: It is in NP and every other problem in NP can be reduced to it in polynomial time
questions.explanation: NP-complete problems are the 'hardest' problems in NP: they are in NP, and any NP problem can be polynomial-time reduced to them, so a polynomial solution to one would solve all of NP.

questions.question: Which of the following is a classic example of an NP-complete problem?
options: The Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT)
Sorting an array of integers
Finding the shortest path in a graph with non-negative weights
Binary search in a sorted array
questions.correct_answer: The Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT)
questions.explanation: SAT was the first problem proven NP-complete (Cook-Levin theorem), and it serves as the basis for proving other problems NP-complete via polynomial-time reductions.

questions.question: The Cook-Levin theorem is historically significant because it established that:
options: SAT is NP-complete, providing the first proof that an NP-complete problem exists
P equals NP conclusively
All problems can be solved in polynomial time
Sorting algorithms cannot run faster than O(n log n)
questions.correct_answer: SAT is NP-complete, providing the first proof that an NP-complete problem exists
questions.explanation: The Cook-Levin theorem (1971) proved that the Boolean satisfiability problem is NP-complete, laying the foundation for the theory of NP-completeness and subsequent reductions.

questions.question: The Traveling Salesman Problem (decision version) is NP-complete. What does this imply for practical solving of large instances?
options: No known polynomial-time algorithm solves it exactly, so heuristics or approximation algorithms are often used for large instances
It can always be solved instantly regardless of input size
It has no valid solution for any input
It can be solved in O(n) time with a simple loop
questions.correct_answer: No known polynomial-time algorithm solves it exactly, so heuristics or approximation algorithms are often used for large instances
questions.explanation: Because TSP is NP-hard, exact algorithms have exponential worst-case time, so practitioners commonly use approximation algorithms or heuristics like nearest-neighbor or genetic algorithms for large instances.

questions.question: What is the goal of an 'approximation algorithm' for an NP-hard optimization problem?
options: To find a solution that is provably close to optimal within polynomial time, even if not exactly optimal
To find the exact optimal solution regardless of time taken
To randomly guess a solution with no guarantees
To only work on small graphs with fewer than 10 vertices
questions.correct_answer: To find a solution that is provably close to optimal within polynomial time, even if not exactly optimal
questions.explanation: Approximation algorithms trade optimality for efficiency, providing a solution within a provable factor (approximation ratio) of the optimal value in polynomial time.

questions.question: What is the approximation ratio of the standard greedy algorithm for the Vertex Cover problem that picks both endpoints of an uncovered edge?
options: A 2-approximation
An exact optimal algorithm
A 10-approximation
It provides no guarantee at all
questions.correct_answer: A 2-approximation
questions.explanation: The simple algorithm of repeatedly picking an uncovered edge and adding both endpoints to the cover produces a vertex cover at most twice the size of the optimal one.

questions.question: What characterizes a 'randomized algorithm' such as randomized QuickSort?
options: It makes random choices during execution to achieve good expected performance, even though its worst case may still be poor
It always produces a different, unpredictable final result
It cannot be analyzed for correctness or performance
It only works on already-sorted input
questions.correct_answer: It makes random choices during execution to achieve good expected performance, even though its worst case may still be poor
questions.explanation: Randomized algorithms use randomness (e.g., random pivot selection) to avoid consistently poor performance on adversarial inputs, giving good expected-case behavior.

questions.question: Why does randomized QuickSort achieve expected O(n log n) time even though its worst case is O(n^2)?
options: Randomly selecting the pivot makes it highly unlikely to repeatedly choose consistently bad pivots across all recursive calls
It sorts the array using merge sort internally
It never actually partitions the array
Randomization eliminates the need for comparisons
questions.correct_answer: Randomly selecting the pivot makes it highly unlikely to repeatedly choose consistently bad pivots across all recursive calls
questions.explanation: By choosing pivots randomly, the probability of consistently poor splits (leading to O(n^2)) becomes vanishingly small, so the expected running time over all random choices is O(n log n).

questions.question: What is the longest common subsequence (LCS) problem typically solved with?
options: Dynamic programming, using a table indexed by prefixes of the two sequences
A single greedy pass through both sequences
Sorting both sequences and comparing directly
A minimum spanning tree algorithm
questions.correct_answer: Dynamic programming, using a table indexed by prefixes of the two sequences
questions.explanation: LCS exhibits optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems, solved by building a 2D DP table where each cell represents the LCS length of prefixes of the two input sequences.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of computing the LCS of two strings of length m and n using standard dynamic programming?
options: O(mn)
O(m + n)
O(m log n)
questions.correct_answer: O(mn)
questions.explanation: The standard DP table for LCS has m x n cells, each computed in constant time from previously computed cells, giving O(mn) time.

questions.question: What is a key application of topological sorting in graph algorithms?
options: Ordering tasks with dependencies (a directed acyclic graph) so each task appears before those that depend on it
Finding the shortest cycle in a graph
Determining whether a graph is bipartite
Computing the diameter of a tree
questions.correct_answer: Ordering tasks with dependencies (a directed acyclic graph) so each task appears before those that depend on it
questions.explanation: Topological sorting produces a linear ordering of vertices in a DAG such that for every directed edge u->v, u comes before v, useful for scheduling tasks with prerequisites.

questions.question: Why can topological sorting only be performed on a directed acyclic graph (DAG)?
options: A cycle would create a contradiction where a vertex would need to appear both before and after another vertex in the ordering
Topological sort works on any graph type without restriction
Cycles make the graph disconnected
Topological sort requires the graph to be weighted
questions.correct_answer: A cycle would create a contradiction where a vertex would need to appear both before and after another vertex in the ordering
questions.explanation: If a graph has a cycle, there is no way to linearly order its vertices such that all directed edges point forward, since the cycle forces a circular dependency.

questions.question: What technique does the Rabin-Karp string matching algorithm primarily rely on?
options: Hashing substrings and comparing hash values to quickly rule out non-matches before verifying character by character
Building a full suffix tree of the text before any comparison
Only using brute-force character comparison with no optimization
Sorting all substrings of the text lexicographically
questions.correct_answer: Hashing substrings and comparing hash values to quickly rule out non-matches before verifying character by character
questions.explanation: Rabin-Karp computes a rolling hash of the pattern and each text window, comparing hashes first (cheap) and only verifying characters when hashes match, giving good average-case performance.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the failure function (partial match table) in the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matching algorithm?
options: To avoid re-examining characters already matched by skipping ahead based on the pattern's own internal structure
To generate random test strings for matching
To sort the pattern's characters alphabetically
To compute the hash value of the text
questions.correct_answer: To avoid re-examining characters already matched by skipping ahead based on the pattern's own internal structure
questions.explanation: KMP precomputes a failure function describing the longest proper prefix of the pattern that is also a suffix, allowing the algorithm to skip redundant comparisons and achieve O(n+m) time.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the KMP string matching algorithm for a text of length n and pattern of length m?
options: O(n + m)
O(nm)
O(n log m)
questions.correct_answer: O(n + m)
questions.explanation: KMP achieves linear time by preprocessing the pattern in O(m) and scanning the text in O(n), avoiding the quadratic worst case of naive string matching.

questions.question: In backtracking algorithms (such as solving the N-Queens problem), what is 'pruning' used for?
options: Abandoning a partial solution early once it is determined it cannot possibly lead to a valid or optimal solution
Randomly discarding valid solutions to reduce output size
Increasing the search space to guarantee correctness
Sorting the final list of solutions found
questions.correct_answer: Abandoning a partial solution early once it is determined it cannot possibly lead to a valid or optimal solution
questions.explanation: Pruning cuts off branches of the search tree that violate constraints early, significantly reducing the number of states explored compared to exhaustive search.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between 'branch and bound' and simple backtracking?
options: Branch and bound uses a bounding function to prune branches that cannot improve on the best solution found so far, targeting optimization problems
Branch and bound never prunes any branch of the search tree
Backtracking is only used for sorting algorithms
There is no difference; they are the same technique
questions.correct_answer: Branch and bound uses a bounding function to prune branches that cannot improve on the best solution found so far, targeting optimization problems
questions.explanation: Branch and bound extends backtracking by computing bounds on the best possible solution from a partial state, pruning branches whose bound is worse than the current best known solution.
